clue.text: Hurried to catch sleep missed

indicators.note: to catch means the word for hurried closes around the word for sleep

parts.note: hurried means sped
kip is British slang for sleep

explanation.surface: Someone rushed off to grab a nap and missed it anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sleep' reads as a verb beside 'catch', but it is the noun KIP, British slang for a nap.
explanation.definitionFit: If you skipped a class or a meal, you passed it over, which is what missing it means.

clue.text: Ball's stratum of society

definitions.meaning: a ball is a globe or round body
a social circle or class, as in moving in a higher social world

explanation.surface: A dance is where a certain social class gathers.
explanation.definitionFit: A globe is a round solid, and a person's social range is called their circle or world.

clue.text: Censure statement by self-proclaimed beauty

parts.note: a person proclaiming themselves says I'm, short for I am
a peach is an attractive person, a beauty

explanation.surface: A self-styled beauty's boastful remark draws criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: The statement is 'I'm (a) peach': the speaker calls themselves a beauty.
explanation.definitionFit: To impeach an official is to formally charge them with wrongdoing, a strong censure.

clue.text: One may get loaded, playing poker, with cash

indicators.note: playing means the letters are toyed with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A card player might get loaded playing poker for cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' rearranges POKERCASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A pack animal is a beast of burden on which goods are loaded.

clue.text: Impede one with zero value — unable to do this?

definitions.note: a thing of zero value cannot get any worse, so the clue's own subject could not do this

parts.note: to deter is to hinder or impede
i is the Roman numeral for one
o looks like zero
a rate is a value or price

explanation.surface: Someone worthless is asked whether they could hinder anything at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points back at 'one with zero value': something already worthless cannot worsen.
explanation.definitionFit: To worsen or decline in quality is impossible for something with no value left to lose.

clue.text: Create ornamental edging, look, inside prize

indicators.note: inside means the word for look sits within the word for prize

parts.note: a scalp is a trophy or prize taken from a defeated opponent
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: A dressmaker is told to add decorative edging, look, inside the prize garment.
explanation.walkthrough: A scalp was a trophy taken from a beaten enemy, hence prize; LO is the archaic 'behold'.
explanation.definitionFit: To scallop fabric is to cut its border into a series of curves for decoration.

clue.text: Note part of London with nothing to lose

indicators.note: to lose means a letter is dropped from the London district's name

parts.note: Soho is a district in central London
o resembles zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A bit of London where you have nothing to lose is noted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with nothing to lose' drops an O from SOHO, a London entertainment district.
explanation.definitionFit: In tonic sol-fa this is the fifth degree of the musical scale.

clue.text: Lunatic losing head is persuasive type

indicators.note: losing head means the word for lunatic drops its first letter

parts.note: a lunatic is a madman

explanation.surface: A maniac who loses his head turns out to be very convincing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing head' takes the M off MADMAN.
explanation.definitionFit: An advertising man's job is to persuade the public to buy.

clue.text: Reluctant Scot in his home territory?

parts.note: loth is a spelling of loath, meaning reluctant
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: A Scotsman is reluctant to leave his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: IAN, a common Scottish name, stands for a Scot; the region named is in Scotland around Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Scottish region around Edinburgh, so a fitting homeland for a man called Ian.

clue.text: Garden area -section with almost produced bloomers?

parts.note: a part is a section

indicators.note: almost means the word for blundered loses its last letter

parts.note: a bloomer is a mistake, so producing bloomers is having erred

explanation.surface: A gardener's flowerbed section nearly produced blooms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ERRED to ERRE; bloomers are blunders, not flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: A parterre is a formal ornamental flower garden laid out in patterned beds.

clue.text: Almost expect to scupper game

indicators.note: almost means the word for expect loses its final letter

parts.note: to hope for something is to expect it
to scotch a plan is to scupper or thwart it

explanation.surface: A gloomy forecaster almost expects to see a game ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' cuts HOPE to HOP.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopscotch is a children's playground pastime of hopping through chalked squares.

clue.text: Mum is head of household, not second

indicators.note: not means the letter for second is taken out of the word for head of household

parts.note: the master is the man at the head of a household

explanation.surface: Mother is in charge at home, not playing second fiddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes S from MASTER.
explanation.definitionFit: Mater is Latin for mother, used as old-fashioned British public-school slang for one's mum.

clue.text: Come to admire achievement, in — part

indicators.note: in part says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone comes to admire an achievement, at least partly.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took only 'Come' as the definition, but 'Come to' is the phrase that means arriving at, so 'to' belongs to it.
explanation.definitionFit: To come to a place is to arrive at it, which is reaching it.

clue.text: Tried once, when drunk, to be abstruse

indicators.note: when drunk means the letters of the two words stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker tried, just once, to sound learned while intoxicated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when drunk' rearranges TRIEDONCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Recondite knowledge is obscure and hard to understand, the same as abstruse.

clue.text: Northern natives in canoe, lads capsizing

indicators.note: capsizing means the letters tip over into a new order

explanation.surface: Some boys from the north overturn their canoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capsizing' rearranges INCANOELADS; 'in' is part of the fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Caledonia is the Latin name for Scotland, so its people are natives of the north of Britain.

clue.text: Crunch arboreal bits for him to process?

definitions.text: Crunch arboreal bits for him to process?

indicators.note: to process means the letters are worked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is given woody bits to crunch up and process.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to process' rearranges CRUNCHARBOREAL; the whole clue also describes the job, since such a worker turns bits of trees into fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional woodland craftsman slowly smoulders timber in a kiln to make fuel, so tree bits are his raw material.

clue.text: French article, a food not fit for consumption

parts.note: une is the French feminine indefinite article
table can mean the food provided, as in keeping a good table

explanation.surface: A French dish is declared unfit to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that cannot be eaten is inedible, unfit to consume.

clue.text: Male fool of advanced years treated in parlour

parts.note: an ass is a fool
aged means old, of advanced years

explanation.surface: An old foolish man gets a treatment at a beauty parlour.
explanation.definitionFit: A rubdown given at a parlour is a treatment of the muscles by kneading.

clue.text: Fruit that's got one well

definitions.meaning: two everyday orchard fruits named together
staircases have a stairwell; the phrase is Cockney rhyming slang for stairs

explanation.surface: A piece of fruit that has done rather well for itself.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang, a London habit, replaces a word with a rhyming phrase: this phrase means stairs, and stairs surround a well.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase literally names two fruits and in rhyming slang means stairs, which have a stairwell.

clue.text: Something imaginative with soft rather than loud colour

indicators.note: with introduces the letter brought in to take the other's place
rather than names the letter being replaced by the one for soft

parts.note: a figment is something imagined
f, forte, is the musical direction for loud
p, piano, is the musical direction for soft

explanation.surface: A fanciful idea makes a soft rather than garish colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with soft rather than loud' swaps P for F in FIGMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigment is a substance that gives colour, as in paint.

clue.text: Old county full of potholes?

definitions.meaning: a former English county, the smallest, now restored as a unitary authority
a land full of ruts, a whimsical description of a bumpy road

explanation.surface: A former county whose roads are full of holes.
explanation.walkthrough: RUTLAND is the smallest traditional English county; the second definition splits it as a land of ruts.
explanation.definitionFit: This is England's smallest historic shire, abolished in 1974 and later restored.

clue.text: Metal ruler used by one wielding power

parts.note: lead is a heavy metal
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A metal ruler is used by a powerful person.
explanation.walkthrough: ER is the late Queen's royal cipher, Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A head of a party or group is the person in command.

clue.text: Is this colour wise/not wise?

parts.note: a sage person is wise
green means naive or inexperienced, not wise

explanation.surface: A puzzled painter asks whether this shade signals wisdom or folly.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a soft greyish green shade named after the herb's leaves.

clue.text: Succeed in good school

parts.note: Eton is a famous English public school

explanation.surface: Someone does well at a good school.
explanation.walkthrough: ETON is an elite English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: To prosper or make progress in life is to do well.

clue.text: More tense in audition? The solution's concentration

indicators.note: in audition means the word is heard spoken, its sound giving the entry

parts.note: more tense means tighter

explanation.surface: An actor grows more tense at an audition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in audition' looks like a theatre scene but is the sound signal; 'solution' is chemistry, not the puzzle's answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry, a titre is the measured strength of a dissolved substance found by titration.

clue.text: Visitor supposed to come from America, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the word is taken by its spoken sound

parts.note: Americans say 'I guess' for 'I suppose', so supposed in American usage is guessed

explanation.surface: A visitor is said to have arrived from the United States.
explanation.definitionFit: A guest is someone visiting or staying at another's home.

clue.text: Distinguished group of bosses right

parts.note: a star performer is distinguished or outstanding
a board of directors is the group running a company

explanation.surface: An eminent group of company directors is in the right.
explanation.definitionFit: Starboard is the right-hand side of a ship looking forward.

clue.text: Half the pieces of paper in a book

indicators.note: half means the word for pieces of paper keeps only its first three of six letters

parts.note: sheets are pieces of paper

explanation.surface: Half the pages in a book are missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' cuts SHEETS to its first half; the book is H. Rider Haggard's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: This 1887 adventure novel by H. Rider Haggard is titled with a feminine pronoun.

clue.text: Easing of tension as river falls outside lodge

indicators.note: falls outside means the river's name wraps around the word for lodge

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Scotland and another in Wales and England
to lodge in a tent is to camp, a tent being a temporary lodging

explanation.surface: Tension eases as a river tumbles past a hunting lodge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'falls' suggests waterfalls on the river, but with 'outside' it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Detente is a relaxing of strained relations, especially between nations.

clue.text: Feeble line into transmitter

indicators.note: into means the letter for line goes inside the word for transmitter

parts.note: a sender is a device that transmits signals

explanation.surface: A weak line runs into a radio transmitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' puts L inside SENDER after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Slender chances or means are slight and weak, so feeble.
